cim: Can a Weakening Jobs Report Slow Wall Street’s AI Slide?
cim_eredeti: Can a Weakening Jobs Report Slow Wall Street’s AI Slide?
szoveg_eredeti:
Artificial intelligence stocks have been struggling in Q4, but could the weakening US job market provide a tailwind for the artificial intelligence boom?

The Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology (NASDAQ:AIQ) ETF has recorded a loss of 5.56% since the beginning of the quarter, creating a downward trend following a five-month period of largely sideways movements.

With hyperscalers betting hundreds of billions of dollars on the sustained growth of the industry, there are clear warning signs that the AI frenzy has begun to slow down.

However, at a time when macroeconomic pressures are beginning to take their toll on Wall Street’s more speculative jobs, it appears that a weakening job market could provide a layer of support.

The United States economy added just 29,000 jobs in September, marking a steep decline on the 133,000 that were added in August. Given that expectations had placed last month’s figure closer to 90,000, the shortfall could have a sizeable impact on the Fed’s monetary outlook.

Given that the uncertain interest rate environment is one of the biggest headwinds AI stocks have faced in 2026, the prospect of a cooling economy driven by slower job growth could help to support high-tech stocks.

Prediction market odds for an additional rate hike at the upcoming Federal Reserve meeting at the end of October have already plummeted from highs of around 50% to just 14%, while Federal Reserve President John Williams sees just one more increase in 2026, with no need for further hikes next year.

Despite this, forecasters are factoring in a 35% chance that Trumpflation could drive at least four interest rate hikes over the next year, a move that could significantly impact AI leaders on Wall Street.

With macroeconomic challenges like the war in Iran and trade tariffs still looming large over equities, we may see lower job market growth as a cooling influence that supports the artificial intelligence boom.

Global markets are having to cope with sustained AI losses, with some of Wall Street’s most reliable funds becoming caught up amid the changing investment landscape.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index recorded losses over eight straight sessions through Friday, October 16, in a 16% losing streak that hasn’t been seen since the 2008 financial crash.

This comes despite significant tech interest in AI and growing demand, creating a mismatch between spending and the market response to the ongoing artificial intelligence buildout.

The Magnificent Seven collective of Alphabet (GOOGL), Amazon (AMZN), Apple (AAPL), Meta Platforms (META), Microsoft (MSFT), Nvidia (NVDA), and Tesla (TSLA) have committed more than $725 billion in capex as the AI buildout continues to gather momentum.

As a result, AI stocks are becoming increasingly susceptible to macroeconomic headwinds, even as the underlying metrics appear positive.

One of the biggest catalysts for the recent downturn was hotter-than-expected inflation in the US, which saw higher gas prices caused by the conflict in Iran contribute to a CPI rise of 3.7%, up from 3.4% in August.

For now, the industry itself is well-positioned to shake off bearish market sentiment on a technical level.

Data suggests that there’s no sign of AI growth slowing down. Since Meta’s launch of its Muse AI assistant a month ago, downloads have topped 6.6 million, while the platform has a daily active user base of 1.8 million.

Similar readings show semiconductors are as popular as ever, with a 51% rise in quarterly revenue recorded by TSMC (TSM), while Samsung recorded a ninefold boost to operating profits.

Given that the World Economic Forum is forecasting that AI will contribute $15.7 trillion to the global economy, it’s worth investors keeping in mind the long-term prospects of the technology’s rollout.

However, the short term could see AI creating its own headwinds. The strength of artificial intelligence as a talent acquisition tool could see more high-tech firms look beyond the US job market to fill their talent gaps.

Although spending on AI is still soaring, the long-term potential of the technology is still enough to maintain a bullish outlook for investors. But the short-term picture has been distorted by a series of headwinds.

The inflationary impact of war in Iran means that AI stocks could continue to slide in 2026 as investors hang on every decision that the Federal Reserve makes. However, weaker job market data and strong demand show that it’s best to maintain a bigger-picture outlook when it comes to artificial intelligence.

What’s next for the technology will depend on the Fed, but the future still remains bright for US artificial intelligence stocks.
